config.title: Controlled vs Uncontrolled

intro.title: Controlled vs Uncontrolled
intro.body: In this lesson, you will build a simple form component to understand the difference between controlled and uncontrolled inputs in Angular. You will learn how to manage form data using two approaches: one where Angular's data binding controls the input value (controlled), and another where the DOM holds the state (uncontrolled). The core concepts involve using template reference variables, two-way data binding with ngModel, and event handling. You'll work with TypeScript for logic and Angular's template syntax for the view. By the end, you'll know when to use each pattern for effective form management in your applications.
intro.usecase: In Angular applications, understanding controlled vs uncontrolled patterns is essential for building robust forms and interactive components. For example, controlled inputs are used in registration forms where validation and real-time feedback are required, while uncontrolled inputs work well for simple search filters where immediate state management isn't necessary. This distinction also applies to complex dashboards with collapsible panels or modals that need to track their open/closed state. Mastering both approaches allows developers to choose the right pattern for scenarios like form wizards, data tables with filters, or settings panels based on whether they need Angular's reactive data flow or direct DOM access.

objectives: Implement a controlled form input by binding its value to a component property using Angular's two-way data binding
Construct an uncontrolled form input using Angular's template reference variables to access DOM elements directly
Configure event handlers to update component state when uncontrolled inputs change
Apply the appropriate form control strategy (controlled vs uncontrolled) based on specific use case requirements
Manipulate form data by extracting values from both controlled and uncontrolled input approaches
Initialize form controls with default values using both controlled and uncontrolled implementation patterns
Integrate form validation logic with controlled inputs using Angular's reactive forms approach

steps.title: Import Component and CommonModule from Angular core
steps.instruction: Import Component from '@angular/core' and CommonModule from '@angular/common'.
steps.hint: Use the import keyword followed by the symbol name and the module path in quotes.

seedCode.App.tsx: // Import Component from '@angular/core' and CommonModule from '@angular/common'

steps.expectedOutcome: The necessary Angular decorator and module are imported for building components.
successCriteria: Component is imported from '@angular/core' and CommonModule is imported from '@angular/common'.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close. Make sure you're importing both Component and CommonModule from their correct module paths.
steps.feedbackWrong: Check the import statements. You need to import Component from '@angular/core' and CommonModule from '@angular/common'.

steps.title: Create the main component class with template
steps.instruction: Create a component class named ControlledVsUncontrolledComponent with a @Component decorator. Include a selector of 'app-controlled-vs-uncontrolled' and a template containing a simple heading.
steps.hint: Use the imported Component decorator to define your class. The template can be a simple string with an <h2> element.
steps.expectedOutcome: A component class is defined with the correct decorator, selector, and a basic template.
successCriteria: Component class ControlledVsUncontrolledComponent is created with @Component decorator containing selector 'app-controlled-vs-uncontrolled' and a template with an <h2> element.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track. Make sure you have: 1) a class named ControlledVsUncontrolledComponent, 2) the @Component decorator with selector and template properties, 3) a template containing an <h2> element.
steps.feedbackWrong: The component structure isn't quite right. Review the example: you need to create a class with the @Component decorator containing selector and template properties.

steps.title: Add a class property for controlled input value
steps.instruction: Inside your component class, add a string property called 'controlledValue' and initialize it with an empty string ''.
steps.hint: Add a property declaration in the class body, like 'controlledValue: string = "";'.
steps.expectedOutcome: The component class now has a 'controlledValue' property that can store the current value of a controlled input.
successCriteria: The component class contains a property named 'controlledValue' of type string initialized to an empty string.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You added a property, but check: is it named exactly 'controlledValue', of type string, and initialized to ''?
steps.feedbackWrong: The component class should have a property 'controlledValue: string = "";' to store input value.

steps.title: Add a class property for uncontrolled input reference
steps.instruction: In the ControlledUncontrolledComponent class, add a property called 'uncontrolledInput' using the ViewChild decorator with ElementRef type.
steps.hint: Use @ViewChild decorator to create a reference to a DOM element. The property should be typed as ElementRef.
steps.analogousExample:
// Example: creating a reference to an input element
@ViewChild('inputRef') inputRef!: ElementRef<HTMLInputElement>;
steps.expectedOutcome: The component will have a property ready to hold a reference to an uncontrolled input element.
successCriteria: The component class contains a property named 'uncontrolledInput' decorated with @ViewChild and typed as ElementRef.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close! Make sure you've added the property with the correct decorator and type.
steps.feedbackWrong: The property wasn't added correctly. Check that you used @ViewChild decorator and ElementRef type.

steps.title: Create handler for controlled input change
steps.instruction: Inside the ControlledUncontrolledComponent class, create a method named 'onControlledChange' that takes an event parameter and updates the 'controlledValue' property with the input's current value.
steps.hint: The method should accept an event of type Event, extract the value from the target element, and assign it to 'controlledValue'.
steps.expectedOutcome: The component now has a method that will handle changes to a controlled input field, updating the component state with the new value.
successCriteria: The 'onControlledChange' method is defined in the component class, accepts an Event parameter, and updates the 'controlledValue' property with the input value.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You've started creating the handler method, but make sure it properly extracts the value from the event target and assigns it to 'controlledValue'.
steps.feedbackWrong: The handler method for controlled input changes is not properly implemented. Remember to create a method named 'onControlledChange' that updates the 'controlledValue' property with the input value from the event.

steps.title: Create handler to read uncontrolled input value
steps.instruction: Create a method named 'getUncontrolledValue' in your component class that reads the current value from the 'uncontrolledInput' reference.
steps.hint: Define a method that accesses the 'value' property of the element referenced by 'uncontrolledInput'.
steps.expectedOutcome: The component will have a method that can read the current value from the uncontrolled input reference.
successCriteria: A method named 'getUncontrolledValue' is defined in the component class and returns the 'value' property from 'uncontrolledInput'.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You've created a method, but make sure it accesses the 'value' property of 'uncontrolledInput'.
steps.feedbackWrong: The method isn't defined correctly. Check that you're accessing the 'value' property from the 'uncontrolledInput' reference.

steps.title: Add controlled input field with binding
steps.instruction: Inside the template, add an input element with two-way binding using [(ngModel)] to bind it to the 'controlledValue' property.
steps.hint: Use the ngModel directive with square and round brackets for two-way binding. The input should look like: <input [(ngModel)]="controlledValue" />
steps.expectedOutcome: The template will contain an input element with two-way binding to the controlledValue property.
successCriteria: The input element uses [(ngModel)]="controlledValue" in the template.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You added an input, but it might be missing the two-way binding syntax [(ngModel)] or the correct property name.
steps.feedbackWrong: The input element is not present or doesn't have the required two-way binding.

steps.title: Add uncontrolled input field with reference
steps.instruction: Inside the component's template, add a second input element with a template reference variable named #uncontrolledRef.
steps.hint: Use the same input element syntax as before, but add a template reference variable using the # symbol followed by the variable name.
steps.analogousExample:
<!-- Similar: template reference variable on an input -->
<input type="text" #myInputRef>
steps.expectedOutcome: The template will contain two input elements: one controlled input with two-way binding and one uncontrolled input with a template reference variable.
successCriteria: An input element with type="text" and a template reference variable #uncontrolledRef is added to the template.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You've added an input element, but it's missing the template reference variable. Make sure to include #uncontrolledRef on the input element.
steps.feedbackWrong: The uncontrolled input with template reference hasn't been added correctly. Check that you've added an input element with type="text" and #uncontrolledRef in the template.

steps.title: Add button to read uncontrolled value
steps.instruction: Add a button element in the template that calls the getUncontrolledValue method when clicked.
steps.hint: Use the (click) event binding to call the method. Place the button after the uncontrolled input field.
steps.analogousExample:
// Example: button with click handler
<button (click)="someMethod()">Click me</button>
steps.expectedOutcome: A button appears in the UI that will trigger the uncontrolled value reading when clicked.
successCriteria: A button element with (click)="getUncontrolledValue()" is added to the template.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You added a button, but make sure it calls getUncontrolledValue() when clicked using (click) binding.
steps.feedbackWrong: The button is missing or not properly connected to the getUncontrolledValue method.

steps.title: Display both input values
steps.instruction: Add two paragraph elements in your template to display the current controlledValue and the uncontrolled input value (accessed via uncontrolledInput.value).
steps.hint: Use the double curly braces {{ }} to bind the component properties to the template. For the uncontrolled value, you'll need to access the .value property of the input reference.
steps.expectedOutcome: The template will show two paragraphs: one displaying the real-time controlled input value, and another displaying the current value of the uncontrolled input (which updates only when accessed).
successCriteria: Two paragraph elements are added to the template using {{ }} interpolation to display controlledValue and uncontrolledInput.value
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You've added some display elements, but make sure you have both paragraphs showing controlledValue and uncontrolledInput.value using proper Angular interpolation syntax.
steps.feedbackWrong: The paragraphs aren't displaying the input values correctly. Remember to use {{ }} interpolation to bind component properties to the template.
